title: Can students work part-time in Japan?

sources.name: Immigration Services Agency: permission for students (留学) to work
Immigration Services Agency: permission to engage in activity other than that permitted (資格外活動許可)

slides.title: Can students work part-time in Japan?
slides.body: Yes, with permission. Here are the rules.

slides.title: Get permission first
slides.body: On a student visa (留学), you need “permission to engage in activity other than that permitted” (資格外活動許可) before any paid work.
slides.note: Apply at your regional immigration office. No fee. It can take 2 weeks to 2 months.

slides.title: Up to 28 hours a week
slides.body: During the school term you can work up to 28 hours a week.
slides.note: Count every job together, not each job separately.

slides.title: Long holidays: up to 8 hours a day
slides.body: During your school's long vacation (for example summer or spring break), you can work up to 8 hours a day.
slides.note: Only during the vacation your school sets, not on any day without class.

slides.title: Where you can't work
slides.body: No work at adult entertainment or nightlife businesses (風俗営業 and similar), in any role, even cleaning or washing dishes.
slides.note: Breaking the rules can put your visa at risk.

slides.title: Source
slides.body: Immigration Services Agency of Japan (moj.go.jp/isa)
slides.note: Checked Nov 1, 2026. General information, not visa advice. Check the official site or ask your school.

title: MEXT scholarship: who can apply and how

slides.title: *Free tuition* in Japan: the MEXT scholarship
slides.body: Tuition, airfare and a monthly allowance.
slides.swipe: Swipe to see if you qualify →

slides.title: What you get
slides.body: Tuition is exempted, your round-trip airfare is paid, and you get a monthly allowance.
slides.note: Most categories: about ¥117,000–¥145,000 a month. The exact amount is in the current MEXT guidelines.

slides.title: 7 categories
slides.body: Research · Teacher training · Undergraduate · Japanese studies · College of technology · Specialized training college · Young Leaders Program
slides.note: Choose the one that matches your level and goal.

slides.title: Age limits
slides.body:
Undergraduate, college of technology, specialized training college: under 25
Research, teacher training: under 35
Japanese studies: 18 to 29
slides.note: The exact cut-off date is in each year's guidelines.

slides.title: Two ways to apply
slides.body:
Embassy: through the Japanese embassy or consulate in your country (documents and interview).
University: through a Japanese university that has an exchange agreement with your school.
slides.note: Application periods differ by country. Check your Japanese embassy's website.

slides.title: Source
slides.body: Study in Japan (JASSO): MEXT scholarships
slides.note: Checked Nov 1, 2026. The official MEXT guidelines take priority. General information, not advice.
slides.cta: Comment MEXT for the official links

title: Overtime, night and holiday pay in Japan

sources.name: MHLW: working hours, breaks and holidays
MHLW Aichi Employment Consultation Center: premium pay

slides.title: Are you paid right for *overtime*?
slides.body: Japan's legal minimum extra pay, in 4 slides.

slides.title: Normal hours: 8 a day, 40 a week
slides.body: Work beyond 8 hours a day or 40 hours a week is overtime.
slides.note: Breaks: at least 45 minutes if you work over 6 hours, 1 hour if over 8. At least 1 day off a week.

slides.title: Overtime: +25% or more
slides.body: Every overtime hour is paid at least 25% more than your normal hourly pay.
slides.note: Over 60 overtime hours in a month: at least +50% (all companies since April 2023).

slides.title: Late night: +25% or more
slides.body: Work from 10pm to 5am is paid at least 25% extra.
slides.note: Late-night overtime counts both: at least +50%.

slides.title: Legal day off: +35% or more
slides.body: Work on your legal day off is paid at least 35% extra.
slides.note: Check your payslip (給与明細) every month.

slides.title: Source
slides.body: Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (mhlw.go.jp)
slides.note: Checked Nov 1, 2026. General information, not legal advice. Pay problems? Your local Labour Standards Inspection Office (労働基準監督署) can help, free.

title: Which school is right for you in Japan?

sources.name: Study in Japan (JASSO): Japan's educational system

slides.title: *Which school* is right for you in Japan?
slides.body: Language school, vocational college or university?

slides.title: Japanese language school
slides.body: Many international students start here to learn Japanese before moving on to a college or university.
slides.note: Check that the school can accept students on a student visa.

slides.title: Vocational college (専門学校)
slides.body: Practical skills for a job. Diploma programs take 2 to 3 years; Advanced Diploma programs take 4 years.
slides.note: Programs differ: check each school's entry requirements.

slides.title: University
slides.body:
A Bachelor's degree takes 4 years (6 for medicine, dentistry, veterinary medicine and some pharmacy).
Master's: 2 years. Doctorate: 5 years.
slides.note: Check each university's language and entry requirements.

slides.title: Other options
slides.body:
Junior college: 2 to 3 years (associate degree).
College of technology: international students join from the 3rd year.
slides.note: All higher education starts after 12 years of school.

slides.title: Source
slides.body: Study in Japan (JASSO): Japan's educational system
slides.note: Checked Nov 1, 2026. General information, not advice. Check each school's own requirements.

sources.name: Aichi Labour Bureau (MHLW): annual paid leave

slides.title: Do you get *paid holidays* in Japan?
slides.body: Yes, by law. Here's how it works.

slides.title: After 6 months: 10 days
slides.body: Work 6 months in a row and come to at least 80% of your working days, and you get 10 days of paid leave (有給休暇).
slides.note: You take them by asking your employer.

slides.title: More days over time
slides.body: The number of days goes up with your years at the company.
slides.note: Part-time? Your days depend on how many days a week you're scheduled to work.

slides.title: At least 5 days a year
slides.body: Since April 2019, if you get 10 or more days, your employer must make sure you take at least 5 of them every year.
slides.note: Days you choose yourself count toward the 5.

slides.title: Know your balance
slides.body: Ask how many paid leave days you have left, and plan them like any other holiday.
slides.note: Paid leave means you get your normal pay for that day.

slides.title: Source
slides.body: Aichi Labour Bureau, Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare
slides.note: Checked Nov 1, 2026. General information, not legal advice. Questions? Your local Labour Standards Inspection Office can help, free.

title: Get your working conditions in writing

sources.name: MHLW: written working conditions for foreign workers

slides.title: *No paper?* Read this before you start work
slides.body: Your working conditions should be in writing.

slides.title: Ask for the paper
slides.body: Before you start, your employer should give you your working conditions in writing (労働条件通知書): pay, working hours and holidays.
slides.note: The Ministry has model notices in English and other languages.

slides.title: Where and what job
slides.body: It must say where you'll work and what job you'll do, and how far that can change later.
slides.note: This "scope of change" rule started in April 2024.

slides.title: Contract with an end date?
slides.body: If your contract is fixed-term, it must say whether there's a limit on renewals.
slides.note: Ask about it before you sign.

slides.title: Keep a copy
slides.body: Keep the paper, or a photo of it. If your pay or hours are different, it's your proof.
slides.note: Your local Labour Standards Inspection Office (労働基準監督署) can help, free.

slides.title: Source
slides.body: Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (mhlw.go.jp)
slides.note: Checked Nov 1, 2026. General information, not legal advice.

sources.name: JLPT (Japan Foundation & JEES): N1–N5 level summary

slides.title: JLPT levels and pass marks
slides.body: What N5 to N1 mean, and the scores you need.

slides.title: Five levels, N5 to N1
slides.body:
N5: some basic Japanese
N4: basic Japanese
N3: everyday Japanese, to a certain degree
N2: everyday Japanese, and a variety of situations to a certain degree
N1: Japanese in a variety of situations
slides.note: N5 is the easiest, N1 the hardest.

slides.title: Twice a year
slides.body: In Japan the test is held in July and December. In 2026: Sunday July 5 and Sunday December 6.
slides.note: Outside Japan, some cities hold it only in July or only in December.

slides.title: Pass marks (out of 180)
slides.note: Every level is scored from 0 to 180.

slides.title: Every section counts
slides.body: You also need the minimum score in each section: 19 for each 60-point section, 38 for the 120-point section at N4 and N5.
slides.note: Miss one section's minimum and you fail, even with a high total.

slides.title: Source
slides.body: Japanese-Language Proficiency Test (jlpt.jp)
slides.note: Checked Nov 3, 2026. General information, not advice. Check the official site.

sources.name: Japan National Tourism Organization (JNTO): Japan Visitor Hotline

slides.title: Emergency numbers in Japan
slides.body: Save these before your trip.

slides.title: Police: 110
slides.body: For crime, accidents and anything urgent that needs the police.
slides.note: Free from any phone.

slides.title: Fire and ambulance: 119
slides.body: For fires and medical emergencies.
slides.note: Say where you are as clearly as you can.

slides.title: Japan Visitor Hotline
slides.body:
050-3816-2787 (from overseas: +81-50-3816-2787)
24 hours a day, 365 days a year, in English, Chinese and Korean.
slides.note: Help in accidents, illness and natural disasters, plus general tourist information. In a real emergency, call 110 or 119 first.

slides.title: Source
slides.body: Japan National Tourism Organization (japan.travel)
slides.note: Checked Nov 3, 2026. General information, not advice. Check the official site.

sources.name: Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications: Move in / Move out (foreign residents)

slides.title: Register your address within 14 days
slides.body: The first thing to do after you move in.

slides.title: Who must register
slides.body: Foreign residents with a residence card (and special permanent residents) who have an address in Japan.
slides.note: Not needed for temporary visitors or stays of 3 months or less.

slides.title: Arriving from abroad
slides.body: Go to your city, ward, town or village office within 14 days of moving in. Bring your residence card.
slides.note: No residence card from the airport? Bring your passport.

slides.title: Moving within Japan
slides.body: Report your move-out at your old municipal office and get a Move-out Certificate. Take it to your new office within 14 days of moving in.
slides.note: Moving inside the same city? Just report the change of address.

slides.title: Leaving Japan
slides.body: Report your move-out to your municipal office before you leave.
slides.note: Bring your residence card.

slides.title: Source
slides.body: Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications (soumu.go.jp)
slides.note: Checked Nov 3, 2026. General information, not advice. Check the official site.
